terms.definition: A circle dance of a planet around the imaginary line through the middle of it, called its axis — one full turn is one day.
terms.function: Sets the length of a planet's day: a slow spinner gets a long day, a fast spinner a short one.
terms.whereItIs: The spinning motion of each sphere in the row as it turns around its axis.
terms.whyItMatters: Every planet rotates, and the rate of rotation tells you how long its day is — no exceptions.

terms.definition: The time a planet takes to spin once completely around its axis.
terms.function: Ticks the counter beneath each sphere: Earth 24.0 hours, Mars 24.6, Jupiter 9.9, Mercury ~176 days, Venus ~117 days.
terms.whereItIs: The floating counter beneath each planet sphere.
terms.whyItMatters: The same 'one day' concept returns wildly different numbers across the solar system.

terms.definition: Spinning in the opposite direction from most planets — Venus (and Uranus, tilted far over) does this.
terms.function: Reverses the planet's apparent direction of sunrise: on Venus the Sun rises in the west.
terms.whereItIs: The backward-pointing arrow above Venus's sphere.
terms.whyItMatters: Highlights that spin direction is not a universal rule; the direct sense of day/night can flip.

terms.definition: The invisible line through a planet around which it spins.
terms.function: Defines the poles (north and south) of rotation and the spin plane.
terms.whereItIs: The dashed segment passing through the center of each sphere in the axis overlay.
terms.whyItMatters: The axis of spinning is the fixed-line reference for every day-length measurement.
